This low birth weight, compared to other large-bodied carnivorans, reflects the abbreviated gestation period characteristic of ursids. A female cub that survives to maturity can achieve an ultimate adult wet weight of up to 100,000 grams [Wwi = up to 100,000 grams], although considerable geographic variation exists across the species' range, with northern populations in Canada often reaching heavier masses than their southern counterparts. This substantial divergence between the sexes is established during the prolonged juvenile growth phase, during which males maintain higher rates of daily mass gain than females. The cubs are entirely dependent on maternal milk during the first months of life, and weaning represents a critical nutritional transition, with young bears reaching a wet weight at weaning of 14,050 grams [Wwx = 14,050 grams] before venturing into independent foraging for mast, berries, and faunal prey.

During this pre-weaning phase, which occurs at the same core temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], the cubs transition from a diet of milk to solid foods, gradually learning to identify seasonally available resources.

This slow maturation is offset by an extended reproductive window, as females can continue breeding well into their late teenage years under favorable conditions. The black bear thus exhibits a life history strategy that prioritizes high survival and gradual growth over early reproduction, a pattern that aligns with its status as a large, long-lived mammal occupying a seasonal environment with pronounced resource pulses.

Following the attainment of sexual maturity, female black bears exhibit a modest reproductive output that is tightly constrained by both somatic condition and environmental productivity. As a long-lived species, the black bear possesses a maximum lifespan of 12,045 days [am = 12,045 days] under natural conditions, as documented through long-term mark-recapture studies in protected populations free from heavy hunting pressure at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This longevity, observed at the standard body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], places the black bear among the longest-lived terrestrial Carnivora in North America, with only the brown bear (Ursus arctos) regularly exceeding this value. Such extended lifespans are evolutionarily supported by the species' low annual mortality rates in the absence of anthropogenic threats, as adult bears face few natural predators aside from intraspecific aggression and, rarely, predation by wolves. The long life expectancy allows even slow reproducers to achieve high lifetime fitness, provided that females can survive through multiple breeding seasons. This combination of late maturation, small litters, and exceptional longevity defines the black bear as a classic example of a K-selected life history strategy among terrestrial mammals.
